subject: ENG
label: Grade 11 Science
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 11 Science English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 5 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Prose and poetry from world writers
modules.outcome: analyse theme and voice in two texts
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Prose and poetry from world writers', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: analyse theme and voice in two texts. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Prose and poetry from world writers' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: analyse theme and voice in two texts, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Simile: 'The moon is like a silver coin.' Metaphor: 'The classroom was a zoo.' Imagery: 'the dew-wet grass' appeals to sight and touch. Say what feeling each creates. Method: Model run for 'Prose and poetry from world writers'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Analyse theme and voice in two texts: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Read Text A, a prose extract. 'Every clear night Imran set up the old telescope on the roof. He did not hope to discover anything; he simply liked knowing that the light he saw had left its star long before he was born.' Note the calm, curious third-person voice.

Step 2, Read Text B, a poem. 'The seed knows nothing of the oak. / It cracks, it reaches, it drinks. / Whatever tree it will become / is built in small, blind inches.' Both texts are about patient growth and the wonder of slow processes in nature.

Step 3, Identify the theme of each. Text A: wonder comes from observation and from understanding the vast scale of time. Text B: great things grow from small, unseen steps. Shared theme: patience and wonder in the natural world. Write each in a full sentence and avoid summarising the plot.

Step 4, Analyse voice. Text A's narrator is gentle and reflective, using a long final sentence to echo the long journey of starlight. Text B's speaker is plain and almost scientific, with verbs 'cracks, reaches, drinks', but ends on the tender image 'blind inches'. Compare tone: awe against quiet respect.

Step 5, Write a comparison. 'Both texts present patience as the heart of discovery. In Text A, Imran enjoys the light that left its star "long before he was born", while in Text B the seed grows in "small, blind inches". The first looks outward in space; the second looks inward at growth.'

Step 6, Your turn: why is 'blind' an effective word in Text B? Model answer: It suggests the seed grows without knowing its goal, so growth is shown as patient trust rather than plan. It also gives the plant a human-like vulnerability that makes the reader care.

modules.example: Solved: Passive: 'The cat chased the mouse' becomes 'The mouse was chased by the cat.' Reported: 'I will come,' she said becomes She said that she would come. Modals: 'should' for advice, 'must' for rules. Agreement: 'The list of items is long.' Edit: 'He go to school' becomes 'He goes to school.' Method: Model run for 'Grammar and editing'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Edit text for tense, agreement and clarity: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Edit for tense. In a lab report the method is usually past tense. Wrong: 'We heat the water and record the temperature every minute yesterday.' Correct: 'We heated the water and recorded the temperature every minute.' A general fact stays in the present: 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.'

Step 2, Edit for agreement. 'The results of the experiment is clear.' The subject is 'results', so write 'are clear'. 'Each of the samples were tested' becomes 'was tested'. 'Neither the teacher nor the students was wearing goggles' becomes 'were wearing', and safety goggles should be worn in any practical.

Step 3, Edit for clarity. 'After heating the beaker, the temperature rose.' The temperature did not heat the beaker. Rewrite: 'After we heated the beaker, the temperature rose.' Put the actor next to the action. Also change 'it' to the noun when the reference is unclear: 'the acid reacted with the metal, and the metal dissolved'.

Step 4, Remove wordiness. 'It is a fact that, due to the fact that metals are good conductors, they are able to be used for wires' becomes 'Because metals conduct well, they are used for wires.' Short, exact sentences suit scientific writing. Keep units and numbers precise.

Step 5, Edit a passage. Original: 'The data shows that the plants in light grows taller, and they was measured weekly.' Edited: 'The data show that the plants in light grew taller, and they were measured weekly.' Data is treated as plural in formal science writing, and the past tense suits a completed experiment.

Step 6, Your turn: correct 'The results of the test shows that the mixture were heated too long.' Answer: 'The results of the test show that the mixture was heated too long.' 'Results' is plural so 'show', while 'mixture' is singular so 'was'.

modules.example: Solved: Formal letter: 12 November 2026; The Principal; Subject: request for a library card; 'Respected Sir, I am a student of Class 8...'; Yours faithfully, Aman. Informal: Dear Ria, ... Your friend, Aman. Report: title, date, place, what happened, result, writer's name. Method: Model run for 'Writing: speeches, articles and reports'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Write persuasive and informative pieces: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Set purpose and audience. Task: persuade classmates to reduce waste in the school laboratory and inform the principal by report. Persuasive writing uses appeals and a call to action; informative writing uses neutral facts in a fixed order. Decide on tone: serious and clear for both audiences.

Step 2, Calculate evidence. The recycling bin held 480 kg of paper in the first half of the year and 600 kg in the second: 120 divided by 480 is 25 percent more. If a class of 30 wastes 2 sheets each daily, that is 60 sheets, so in 20 school days 1,200 sheets are wasted.

Step 3, Write the speech. 'Dear friends, imagine twelve hundred sheets of paper vanishing in one month, from one class alone. Our recycling rose by 25 percent this year, so change is possible.' A striking figure, then a hopeful fact, makes listeners want to act.

Step 4, Write a short article. Headline: 'Small Changes, Big Savings in Our Lab'. By-line. Opening: 'Students recycled 600 kg of paper in the second half of the year, 25 percent more than before.' Close with a practical tip, such as printing on both sides.

Step 5, Write a practical lab-safety report paragraph. 'During the experiment, all students wore goggles and tied back long hair. Chemicals were handled with gloves, and spills were reported at once.' Reports state what was done, in past tense and third person, with no personal opinions.

Step 6, Your turn: a class of 25 wastes 3 sheets each day. How many sheets in 10 days? Answer: 25 times 3 is 75 sheets per day, and 75 times 10 is 750 sheets in 10 days. Write it as 'The class wastes 750 sheets in 10 days.'

Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Answer inference and evaluation questions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Read my own passage. "The experiment's results were consistent, yet the researcher hesitated to publish; a single instrument error, she knew, could undo months of work." Gist: she values accuracy over speed.
Step 2, Find evidence for her attitude. "Hesitated" and "could undo months of work" suggest caution and awareness of risk. Reason: the verb and the consequence together reveal attitude.

Step 3, Answer an inference question. "Why does she hesitate?" Model: "She hesitates because she fears an instrument error might invalidate the results; 'could undo months of work' shows the risk is serious."

Step 4, Answer an evaluation question. "How effective is the sentence structure?" Model: "The contrast introduced by 'yet' creates tension between success and doubt, and the long final clause makes the risk feel heavy."

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "She is nervous because she is a scientist." (no evidence) Right: "She is cautious, since she thinks about one instrument error undoing her work." Always anchor an inference in words from the text.

Step 6, Read a poem, my own: "The telescope counts what the night will give: / a cold white scatter, patient, slow." Inference: observation requires patience. Evidence: "patient, slow". Tone: calm, respectful of nature.

Step 7, Your turn. Passage: "The data fit the theory so neatly that the team grew suspicious." What does this suggest? Model answer: "Perfect fit seems unlikely; 'suspicious' shows they suspect error or bias, so they will check their method."

modules.standard: Deliver a structured speech and respond to questions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Plan a structured speech. Topic: "Why scientific literacy matters." Thesis: "Citizens need scientific literacy to judge evidence and make informed decisions." Structure: hook, thesis, three points, counter-view, conclusion.

Step 2, Write the hook and thesis. "During the last flu season, a false claim about a cure spread faster than the virus. Scientific literacy is the best protection against such claims." Reason: a real-world hook shows relevance.

Step 3, Develop a point with evidence. "First, literacy helps people judge sources. A claim from a controlled trial deserves more trust than a single story." Reason: contrast shows how to test reliability.

Step 4, Handle the counter-view. "Some argue that experts should decide. Experts matter, but citizens vote and choose; they need to understand evidence to hold decisions accountable." Reason: a rebuttal strengthens the speech.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "Science is cool and everyone should like it." Better: "Science teaches a method of testing claims, and that method improves everyday decisions." Replace opinion words with precise benefits.

Step 6, Respond to a question. Q: "Does everyone need to know the details?" A: "No, but everyone should understand how evidence is gathered and tested; that is the core skill." Reason: concede, then clarify.

Step 7, Your turn. Write a thesis and one rebuttal for a speech on "Renewable energy investment". Model answer: "Thesis: Investing in renewables secures long-term energy and cleaner air." "Rebuttal: Initial costs are high, but lower running costs repay them over time."
